talks.title: Deceptacon: Wireless Deception and Evasion
talks.teaser: Techniques for wireless deception and evasion during penetration tests and red team operations.
talks.summary:
### Introducing the Deceptacon Wireless Framework
At 00:00, Vivek Ramachandran, Nishant Sharma, and Ashish Bhangale present Deceptacon, an advanced wireless deception, evasion, and covert communication framework targeting 802.11 Wi-Fi networks and monitoring architectures.

### Covert Micro-Frame Signaling and Wireless Steganography
At 07:02, the presenters explain how 802.11 management frames can be repurposed as high-throughput covert communication channels. By embedding hidden data payloads directly into beacon frames, probe requests, and probe responses, IoT devices and rogue implants can exchange command-and-control telemetry without establishing standard IP connections.

### Embedded Firmware Engineering on ESP8266 Hardware
At 14:14, the team showcases custom firmware implementations running on low-cost ESP8266 microcontrollers. They detail how raw frame injection and promiscuous packet capture can be executed reliably on constrained microcontrollers, turning ubiquitous hardware into powerful wireless reconnaissance and deception nodes.

### Bypassing and Disrupting Enterprise WIPS
At 21:22, the speakers demonstrate active deception techniques against Wireless Intrusion Prevention Systems (WIPS). By dynamically generating hundreds of virtual access points, spoofing BSSIDs, and rapidly modulating channel parameters, Deceptacon floods monitoring sensors with deceptive telemetry, exhausting sensor processing queues and masking unauthorized rogue APs.

### In-Memory Execution and Autonomous Red-Team Operations
Concluding between 28:01 and 35:01, the authors explore stealth operational tactics. By executing payload generation and covert mesh routing entirely within volatile RAM, field-deployed nodes leave zero physical storage forensics, providing red teams with autonomous, battery-efficient tools for prolonged wireless evasion engagements.

talks.title: Failsafe: Yet Another SimpliSafe Attack Vector
talks.teaser: Exploitation techniques against SimpliSafe home security systems via wireless attack vectors.
talks.summary:
### Physical and Wireless Attack Surfaces in Consumer Security
At 00:00, security researcher Nick DePetrillo examines wireless physical security weaknesses in SimpliSafe consumer home alarm systems at the Wireless Village. He discusses the growing reliance of residential security on unencrypted, low-power radio frequency protocols.

### Radio Reconnaissance on ISM Bands
At 13:12, DePetrillo explains his methodology for reverse-engineering SimpliSafe keypad and sensor communications. Operating across the 433 MHz and 315 MHz ISM bands, he reveals that early SimpliSafe hardware communicates in unencrypted, unauthenticated radio packets between window/door contacts, base stations, and keypads.

### Replay Attacks and Packet Injection via Software-Defined Radio
At 26:39, the speaker demonstrates how low-cost Software-Defined Radio (SDR) hardware (such as RTL-SDR and the Yard Stick One) can capture wireless transmission sequences. By analyzing recorded signal waveforms, he constructs Python scripts to forge alarm state messages and replay legitimate disarm transmissions.

### Cleartext PIN Interception and Silent System Disarming
At 39:40, DePetrillo demonstrates the capture of cleartext administrative PIN codes transmitted by keypads during daily operation. An adversary stationed outside a property can intercept the passcode over the air, spoof a valid disarm command, and suppress alarm notifications without notifying the homeowner or monitoring station.

### Engineering Mitigations: Cryptographic Authentication and Rolling Codes
Concluding around 45:00, DePetrillo contrasts insecure static radio packets with robust wireless cryptographic standards. He stresses that consumer alarm manufacturers must implement rolling code mechanisms, cryptographic message authentication (such as AES-CCM), and secure key exchange to prevent unauthorized interception.

talks.title: Large Scale Wireless Monitoring: KISMET Packet Sniffer
talks.teaser: Large-scale wireless network monitoring and analysis using the KISMET packet sniffer tool.
talks.summary:
### Architectural Principles of Large-Scale Wireless Monitoring
At 00:00, Alexander Zakarov (ALFTEL Systems) presents an engineering framework for high-throughput, multi-radio 802.11 packet capture and RF spectrum analysis utilizing the open-source Kismet wireless sniffer.

### Overcoming Single-Radio Channel Hopping Bottlenecks
Zakarov analyzes the fundamental physical limitations of traditional single-radio packet sniffing. Because 802.11 networks operate across dozens of 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz channels, a single radio must rapidly hop frequencies, causing severe packet loss and missing transient client probe requests, handshake authentications, and management beacons.

### High-Density Multi-Radio Hardware: The ALFTEL Airbud
The presentation showcases the ALFTEL Airbud appliance, a specialized multi-interface wireless platform equipped with eight independent radio cards. Zakarov details how dedicated hardware antennas and PCIe interconnects provide concurrent multi-channel visibility without dropping frames under heavy RF saturation.

### Distributed Radio Role Allocation in Modern Kismet
Zakarov explores the architectural enhancements in modern Kismet releases that support distributed multi-device orchestration. The software dynamically partitions radio cards into specialized functional roles—allocating dedicated interfaces to continuous capture on high-traffic channels while assigning auxiliary radios to passive wideband discovery and device tracking.

### Operational Deployment and Spectrum Intelligence
The session concludes with practical strategies for enterprise deployments. By feeding multi-source RF telemetry into centralized analysis pipelines, network defenders and researchers can continuously track rogue devices, map physical access point density, and identify unauthorized wireless bridges across expansive campus environments.
